title: Act when focal symptoms resolve
stem: A client's unilateral arm weakness and difficulty speaking resolve after ten minutes. They now want to resume routine activities. What is most appropriate?
options: Schedule routine review only if the same symptoms recur
Use normal current strength to cancel the event report
Assess only blood pressure before clearing usual activity
Arrange urgent stroke/TIA assessment despite recovery
why: Waiting for recurrence can delay investigation and prevention.
A normal examination now does not negate the observed focal episode.
One measurement cannot determine the cause or safety of the episode.
Transient deficits can signal a time-sensitive vascular event and future stroke risk.
takeaway: Transient deficits can signal a time-sensitive vascular event and future stroke risk.
learningObjective: Arrange urgent assessment for a transient focal neurological deficit despite apparent recovery.

title: Recognize a possible posterior circulation event
stem: A client suddenly develops severe imbalance, vomiting and double vision. Hand grasps remain equal. What should the nurse do?
options: Activate urgent neurological assessment for possible stroke
Give a motion-sickness medicine and wait for improvement first
Exclude stroke because both hands are equally strong
Assist repeated walking trials to distinguish anxiety from imbalance
why: Posterior circulation events may affect balance and vision without unilateral arm weakness.
Symptom relief must not delay assessment of sudden focal neurological features.
A limited motor screen cannot exclude all stroke locations.
Testing unsafe walking delays evaluation and increases injury risk.
takeaway: Posterior circulation events may affect balance and vision without unilateral arm weakness.
learningObjective: Consider stroke when sudden balance and coordination symptoms occur without typical arm weakness.

title: Escalate a thunderclap headache
stem: A client with occasional migraines reports a new headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds and feels unlike previous headaches. What is the priority?
options: Ask the client to keep a one-week headache diary first
Urgent assessment for an acute intracranial cause
Use the usual migraine plan and reassess after sleep
Wait for weakness before arranging emergency assessment
why: A diary is useful for stable recurrent symptoms, not this acute warning pattern.
Sudden maximal onset and a changed pattern require investigation for serious pathology.
Prior migraine history does not establish the cause of this different headache.
Dangerous intracranial bleeding may initially present without focal weakness.
takeaway: Sudden maximal onset and a changed pattern require investigation for serious pathology.
learningObjective: Recognize an abrupt maximal-intensity headache as an emergency rather than assuming usual migraine.

title: Recognize delayed head-injury deterioration
stem: A client initially spoke normally after a head injury but is now increasingly difficult to arouse and repeatedly vomiting. What is appropriate?
options: Treat vomiting before deciding whether neurological review is needed
Use the initial normal conversation as the baseline for discharge
Activate urgent reassessment for evolving intracranial injury
Allow uninterrupted sleep because fatigue followed the injury
why: Antiemetic treatment must not delay assessment of declining consciousness.
Disposition must reflect the current deterioration, not the earlier state.
Delayed decline can reflect secondary injury despite an initially reassuring interval.
Progressive impaired arousal is not ordinary post-event tiredness.
takeaway: Delayed decline can reflect secondary injury despite an initially reassuring interval.
learningObjective: Interpret a decline after initial alertness as possible evolving intracranial injury.

title: Assess comprehension despite expressive aphasia
stem: After a stroke, a client struggles to produce words but follows demonstrated commands accurately. What approach best assesses understanding?
options: Score all unanswered verbal questions as disorientation
Ask only the family because the client cannot speak fluently
Repeat questions progressively louder without changing the response method
Use short statements and reliable yes/no or pointing responses
why: Expressive difficulty can prevent speech despite preserved comprehension.
The client can still participate through suitable communication methods.
Louder speech does not address an expressive language deficit.
Alternative response methods reduce the effect of impaired speech production.
takeaway: Alternative response methods reduce the effect of impaired speech production.
learningObjective: Separate impaired speech production from inability to understand during neurological assessment.

title: Identify neurological deterioration from baseline
stem: A client is under observation after an intracranial event. Which findings represent concerning changes from the documented baseline? Select all that apply.
options: An unchanged pupil difference documented before admission
The same longstanding hand tremor without functional change
New difficulty staying awake during assessment
New unilateral weakness compared with the previous examination
A pupil becomes newly larger and poorly reactive
why: A stable pre-existing asymmetry is less concerning than a new change.
An unchanged chronic finding does not by itself establish acute deterioration.
A declining level of consciousness can indicate worsening brain function.
A new focal deficit requires timely neurological assessment.
A new pupil change can indicate evolving intracranial compromise.
takeaway: A declining level of consciousness can indicate worsening brain function.
learningObjective: Select new neurological changes that warrant escalation rather than stable pre-existing findings.

title: Escalate a prolonged seizure
stem: A generalized seizure continues beyond the client's documented emergency rescue threshold. The nurse is competent and authorized to follow that plan. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the prescribed rescue medicine according to the plan
Wait for spontaneous recovery before alerting the team
Give the next routine oral antiseizure tablet during convulsions
Restart timing each time limb movements briefly lessen
Activate the emergency response while supporting airway safety
why: The established threshold authorizes timely rescue treatment rather than continued waiting.
This delays the response specified for a prolonged seizure.
Oral administration is unsafe and does not substitute for the rescue route.
Brief fluctuation does not necessarily mark recovery or a new event.
Prolonged seizure activity needs prompt assistance and physiological support.
takeaway: Prolonged seizure activity needs prompt assistance and physiological support.
learningObjective: Activate emergency treatment when seizure duration exceeds the prescribed rescue threshold.

title: Recognize seizures without recovery
stem: A client has another convulsive seizure before regaining consciousness from the first. What is the priority interpretation?
options: Separate minor events that can each be reviewed routinely
A reason to postpone assessment until the client can describe symptoms
A continuing seizure emergency requiring urgent escalation
An expected postictal pattern that needs only quiet rest
why: Lack of recovery between events increases urgency.
Current emergency care cannot wait for a verbal history.
Repeated seizures without recovery can threaten ventilation and neurological function.
A further seizure before recovery is not ordinary postictal sleep.
takeaway: Repeated seizures without recovery can threaten ventilation and neurological function.
learningObjective: Distinguish recurrent seizures without return to baseline from a single resolving postictal period.

title: Evaluate postictal recovery
stem: After a brief seizure, which findings support recovery toward baseline? Select all that apply.
options: The client becomes harder to arouse at each check
A new unilateral weakness persists on repeated checks
Another seizure begins before consciousness returns
Breathing is regular with a maintained airway
The client becomes progressively more responsive and oriented
why: Progressive loss of responsiveness needs urgent reassessment.
A persistent focal change warrants neurological evaluation rather than assumed routine recovery.
Recurrence without recovery indicates a seizure emergency.
Stable ventilation is necessary during the recovery period.
Improvement over serial assessments supports resolving postictal effects.
takeaway: Stable ventilation is necessary during the recovery period.
learningObjective: Use airway status and improving mentation to distinguish recovery from continuing deterioration.

title: Document a possible focal seizure
stem: A client suddenly stops responding, makes repetitive chewing movements for one minute and later cannot recall the event. What is most useful to report?
options: The onset, observed movements, responsiveness and recovery pattern
A conclusion that the client refused to cooperate
Only that the client appeared anxious beforehand
Only the normal behaviour after the episode ended
why: A precise description supports evaluation for a focal impaired-awareness seizure.
That labels intent without explaining the sudden stereotyped episode.
The event's neurological features and timing are central to assessment.
Normal later behaviour does not capture the event requiring evaluation.
takeaway: A precise description supports evaluation for a focal impaired-awareness seizure.
learningObjective: Describe observed behaviour and recovery without assuming deliberate nonparticipation.

title: Recognize bulbar weakness in myasthenia
stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is being reassessed. Which changes require prompt evaluation for a possible crisis? Select all that apply.
options: The usual mild evening eyelid droop is unchanged
Hand strength matches the documented baseline
The voice becomes weak and speech trails off after a few words
The cough becomes weak and saliva is difficult to clear
Breathing becomes shallow with visible fatigue
why: An established stable ocular symptom is less urgent than new bulbar or respiratory decline.
Unchanged limb strength does not itself indicate new crisis.
Fatiguing bulbar function can accompany significant neuromuscular weakness.
Reduced clearance threatens airway protection.
Respiratory muscle weakness can lead to ventilatory failure.
takeaway: Fatiguing bulbar function can accompany significant neuromuscular weakness.
learningObjective: Identify changes suggesting airway-protection or respiratory risk during myasthenia gravis.

title: Assess ventilation during Guillain-Barré progression
stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has spreading weakness and difficulty taking a deep breath, but saturation remains 97%. What is appropriate?
options: Encourage repeated exhausting deep-breathing trials before reporting
Wait for cyanosis before arranging higher-level review
Urgent respiratory assessment including muscle-function measures as ordered
Use saturation alone to continue routine observation
why: Fatiguing a weakening client can delay needed respiratory support.
Cyanosis is a late and unreliable trigger for escalation.
Neuromuscular ventilation can worsen before pulse oximetry falls.
Oximetry does not directly measure respiratory muscle strength or ventilation.
takeaway: Neuromuscular ventilation can worsen before pulse oximetry falls.
learningObjective: Recognize respiratory muscle decline despite initially preserved oxygen saturation.

title: Recognize autonomic instability with Guillain-Barré
stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome develops marked fluctuations in pulse and blood pressure. Which nursing responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Treat a normal single reading as proof the problem resolved
Report possible autonomic involvement promptly
Continue the ordered cardiac and blood-pressure monitoring
Interpret every pressure rise as pain without reassessment
Stop observations during sleep to obtain an undisturbed baseline
why: Intermittent normal values do not exclude recurrent autonomic episodes.
The disease can affect autonomic control and produce cardiovascular instability.
Trend monitoring can detect clinically important rhythm and pressure changes.
Autonomic dysfunction can produce fluctuations independent of pain.
Instability can occur during sleep and still needs monitoring.
takeaway: The disease can affect autonomic control and produce cardiovascular instability.
learningObjective: Identify cardiovascular changes requiring monitoring during acute peripheral nerve dysfunction.

title: Investigate a reversible trigger of worsening weakness
stem: A client with multiple sclerosis develops worse weakness during fever and urinary symptoms. Which assessments are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assume permanent disease progression from this episode alone
Begin a strenuous strengthening session to test remaining capacity
Withhold reporting until the fever has fully resolved
Compare the neurological findings with the established baseline
Assess for infection and obtain ordered specimens
why: An acute reversible trigger must be considered.
Exertional fatigue during acute illness can worsen function and adds little immediate safety information.
Significant new weakness still requires timely assessment.
The change and its severity guide urgency and further investigation.
Infection and fever can worsen existing neurological symptoms.
takeaway: The change and its severity guide urgency and further investigation.
learningObjective: Assess fever and infection before attributing all new multiple-sclerosis symptoms to progression.

title: Respond to autonomic dysreflexia
stem: A client with a high spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing and blood pressure far above baseline. The urinary catheter tubing is kinked. What is appropriate?
options: Document the pressure as the client's new baseline
Initiate the dysreflexia protocol and promptly relieve the visible kink
Treat the headache first and recheck the tubing at the next round
Lay the client flat because headache suggests reduced perfusion
why: A sudden symptomatic rise after high spinal injury is not a routine adaptation.
Bladder distension can trigger dangerous hypertension requiring immediate action and monitoring.
Delaying trigger removal may permit ongoing hypertensive injury.
Flat positioning can worsen the hypertension in autonomic dysreflexia.
takeaway: Bladder distension can trigger dangerous hypertension requiring immediate action and monitoring.
learningObjective: Recognize a hypertensive emergency pattern after high spinal injury and address triggers under protocol.

title: Recognize cauda equina warning symptoms
stem: A client with back pain develops urinary retention and numbness around the perineum. What is the priority?
options: Treat retention alone and assume the back problem is unchanged
Wait for complete leg paralysis before escalating
Urgent assessment for possible cauda equina compression
Arrange a routine physiotherapy appointment for back strengthening
why: The neurological pattern needs assessment beyond isolated bladder drainage.
Waiting for further loss can delay treatment of a neurological emergency.
The combination suggests threatened sacral nerve function requiring time-sensitive evaluation.
Routine musculoskeletal care is insufficient for new bladder and saddle symptoms.
takeaway: The combination suggests threatened sacral nerve function requiring time-sensitive evaluation.
learningObjective: Escalate new bladder dysfunction and saddle sensory loss with back pain.

title: Escalate new deficits after spinal surgery
stem: After spinal surgery, a client develops new bilateral leg weakness and loss of bladder control. These were absent on return from recovery. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure that the same deficits are expected after any spinal operation
Assist walking to determine whether the weakness resolves
Wait for the next analgesic dose before repeating assessment
Urgently report and reassess the new neurological deficits
why: New changes from postoperative baseline cannot be assumed routine.
Mobilization is unsafe before evaluating the new deficit.
Analgesia timing should not delay evaluation of neurological loss.
An acute compressive or other surgical complication may require rapid intervention.
takeaway: An acute compressive or other surgical complication may require rapid intervention.
learningObjective: Recognize acute postoperative neurological change as a possible compressive complication.

title: Prioritize suspected meningitis deterioration
stem: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and increasing difficulty staying awake. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Urgent physiological assessment and escalation for suspected CNS infection
Complete a detailed lifestyle headache diary first
Wait for a diagnostic rash before activating care
Treat the pain as the sole problem because neck stiffness is present
why: Declining alertness with this symptom cluster requires immediate review and support.
A diary does not address the current systemic and neurological deterioration.
A rash is not required for serious meningitis or encephalitis.
Pain control does not replace assessment of infection and reduced consciousness.
takeaway: Declining alertness with this symptom cluster requires immediate review and support.
learningObjective: Recognize fever with meningeal and consciousness changes as an urgent physiological problem.

title: Protect a possible CSF leak
stem: After head trauma, a client develops new clear nasal drainage. A skull-base injury is suspected. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Pack the nostril tightly to stop the fluid
Insert nasal suction to determine the drainage source
Treat a bedside glucose strip as definitive proof of CSF
Report the drainage and follow the diagnostic collection plan
Discourage nose blowing while awaiting assessment
why: Packing can obstruct drainage and introduce trauma or infection.
Nasal instrumentation may be hazardous with suspected skull-base injury.
A nonspecific bedside glucose result cannot confirm the diagnosis.
The team needs to evaluate a possible cerebrospinal-fluid leak.
Increased nasal pressure may worsen leakage or introduce complications.
takeaway: The team needs to evaluate a possible cerebrospinal-fluid leak.
learningObjective: Avoid obstructing or traumatizing new clear nasal drainage after head injury.

title: Recognize possible shunt malfunction
stem: A child with a ventricular shunt develops repeated vomiting, headache and unusual sleepiness. The caregiver says this is not the child's usual behaviour. What is appropriate?
options: Wait for swelling over the shunt tubing to appear
Recommend sleep at home and review the next day
Urgent neurological and shunt assessment
Treat the vomiting as gastroenteritis before reviewing the shunt history
why: A malfunction may occur without visible swelling.
Increasing sleepiness can represent deterioration needing earlier care.
The symptoms may reflect impaired CSF drainage and raised intracranial pressure.
The device and neurological changes require consideration of malfunction.
takeaway: The symptoms may reflect impaired CSF drainage and raised intracranial pressure.
learningObjective: Escalate new vomiting and neurological decline in a child with a cerebrospinal-fluid shunt.

title: Interpret an infant's neurological warning pattern
stem: An infant is febrile, feeds poorly and has a bulging fontanelle while calm and upright. What is the best response?
options: Reassess only after a longer crying episode
Treat feeding difficulty as the only current issue
Reassure because fontanelles normally remain open in infancy
Arrange urgent assessment for possible intracranial infection or pressure
why: Crying can increase fullness and does not clarify this already concerning finding.
The neurological and systemic signs require a broader urgent assessment.
An open fontanelle does not make persistent bulging with illness normal.
Persistent bulging with systemic illness is concerning, unlike transient fullness during crying.
takeaway: Persistent bulging with systemic illness is concerning, unlike transient fullness during crying.
learningObjective: Distinguish a concerning bulging fontanelle pattern from transient fullness during crying.

title: Consider an organic cause of acute behavioural change
stem: A previously independent adult develops fever, new bizarre behaviour and a first seizure. What should guide initial care?
options: Urgent medical assessment for an acute brain or systemic process
Assume a primary psychiatric relapse without a neurological assessment
Focus only on de-escalation and postpone vital signs
Interpret the seizure as voluntary because behaviour is unusual
why: Infection or other physiological disease can cause abrupt behavioural and seizure changes.
No prior psychiatric pattern explains away fever and a first seizure.
Safety communication should accompany, not replace, physiological assessment.
Observed behaviour does not justify dismissing a possible neurological emergency.
takeaway: Infection or other physiological disease can cause abrupt behavioural and seizure changes.
learningObjective: Identify fever and new seizures as cues requiring medical assessment of behavioural change.

title: Escalate transient monocular vision loss
stem: A client reports a painless dark curtain over one eye for several minutes that has now resolved. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to record events for several weeks before reporting
Urgent assessment despite return of vision
Schedule routine glasses testing as the first response
Reassure because persistent blindness did not develop
why: Waiting may delay investigation of a warning vascular event.
Transient monocular loss may indicate retinal ischemia or another serious cause.
A refractive assessment does not address abrupt transient visual loss.
Resolution does not exclude a time-sensitive underlying process.
takeaway: Transient monocular loss may indicate retinal ischemia or another serious cause.
learningObjective: Recognize sudden one-eye visual loss as requiring urgent vascular and ophthalmic assessment.

title: Recognize acute angle-closure symptoms
stem: A client has sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision with halos, headache and vomiting. What should happen?
options: Cover the eye and schedule review when vomiting settles
Recommend routine lubricating drops and reassess tomorrow
Arrange emergency eye assessment
Use the usual migraine plan without examining the eye complaint
why: Symptom masking and delay can threaten vision.
Lubrication does not treat acute intraocular pressure elevation.
This combination can indicate an acute pressure-related eye emergency.
Ocular pain and halos require evaluation beyond a presumed headache diagnosis.
takeaway: This combination can indicate an acute pressure-related eye emergency.
learningObjective: Identify an acute painful visual-disturbance pattern requiring emergency eye assessment.

title: Respond to retinal-detachment warning symptoms
stem: A client develops new flashes, many floaters and a shadow spreading across one eye's vision, without pain. What is most appropriate?
options: Arrange a routine refraction appointment next month
Wait for redness or eye pain to confirm severity
Advise screen rest as the main treatment
Urgent ophthalmic assessment for possible retinal detachment
why: A refractive problem does not explain this acute retinal warning pattern.
Retinal detachment may remain painless and externally quiet.
Rest does not reattach a threatened retina or replace urgent assessment.
Retinal separation can threaten vision despite painless symptoms.
takeaway: Retinal separation can threaten vision despite painless symptoms.
learningObjective: Escalate new flashes, floaters and a visual-field curtain despite absent pain.
